title: Berkshire 2009 letter: float, inverted thinking, stock deals, and buying in a panic
summary: Buffett restates how Berkshire measures itself, what it avoids (unknowable industries, dependence on outsiders, bureaucracy), how insurance float works, and why issuing undervalued stock is costly. He admits the GEICO credit card and NetJets blunders and urges buying big when fear is high.

principles.text: Avoid businesses whose long-term economics you can't evaluate, however exciting the growth.
principles.quote: Just because Charlie and I can clearly see dramatic growth ahead for an industry does not mean we can judge what its profit margins and returns on capital will be as a host of competitors battle for supremacy.

principles.text: Never depend on outsiders; hold liquidity that dwarfs any cash need, even at a steep cost.
principles.quote: We will never become dependent on the kindness of strangers.

principles.text: Insurance float is free money if you underwrite profitably; the industry usually pays to hold it.
principles.quote: If we do so, our float will be cost-free, much as if someone deposited $62 billion with us that we could invest for our own benefit without the payment of interest.

principles.text: Issuing undervalued stock to buy a business destroys value for your own shareholders.
principles.quote: You simply can't exchange an undervalued stock for a fully-valued one without hurting your shareholders.

principles.text: Fear is an investor's friend; when opportunities are huge, act big.
principles.quote: When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.

principles.text: Focus on what you pay for a business and what it earns over the next decade or two.
principles.quote: In the end, what counts in investing is what you pay for a business – through the purchase of a small piece of it in the stock market – and what that business earns in the succeeding decade or two.
